newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Britain's Co-op Bank ups profit, not for sale.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Britain's Co-op Bank ups profit, not for sale.

text.p: Britain's Co-operative Bank Plc, under a takeover shadow, said on Wednesday its annual pretax profits rose by 24 percent to 45.5 million pounds ($75 million).

Known for its ethical and environmental stance, the smallest of Britain's clearing banks -- with only three percent of the market -- is a wholly owned subsidiary of the Co-operative Wholesale Society (CWS), which has said it is not up for sale.

Entrepreneur Andrew Regan's Lanica Trust said in February that it had made an approach to the CWS "to discuss the possible puchase of certain non-food businesses". The CWS's interests range from insurance to funeral parlours and travel agencies.
But the Co-op Bank's managing director Terry Thomas told Reuters it was not up for grabs. "The board and our parent company's board have said that our company is not for sale," he said.
Retail deposits with the bank are now double their level five years ago, retail lending has risen 16 percent and total assets have risen to 4.5 billion pounds.
"We are capturing more market share," said Thomas, who retires from the bank later this year.
He said nothing should be read into a proposed increase in the Co-op's share capital, which was agreed by the CWS before the emergence of the Regan attempt to buy its non-food businesses.

He said the parent could inject new capital into the bank whenever it liked, although it had not done so for the past 10 years. By reinvesting five million pounds in the bank's capital, it was indicating it regarded it as a core business, he added.
The capital increase was a prudent step needed to ensure the bank was not restricted in its growth, which was expected to continue to be strong.
Thomas said the Co-op, which has expanded in recent years, was not complacent and was investing heavily so it could compete in the next century.
This involved being able to provide an "anytime, anywhere banking service" demanded by "increasingly sophisticated individual and corporate customers".
He said this investment meant considerable capital and revenue spending and a higher cost-income ratio but that such expenditure could be "throttled back at any time if the need arose".

The Co-op's provisions for bad and doubtful debts in the year ended January 11 1997 rose to 23.7 million pounds from 22.7 million in 1995 but Thomas said he was not worried by this as it reflected a rise in personal lending and the addition of two new products.

These were a variable rate loan and the Co-op's Advantage Visa card, which the bank says offers the lowest-ever credit card interest rate in Britain. The card, launched last year, has more than 50,000 customers already, the bank said.
Thomas said the bank had not seen any evidence of so-called "carpet-baggers" opening accounts in anticipation of some sort of pay-back in the event of a successful takeover of the bank.

He said he had received letters from concerned customers but had not had any in favour of Regan's proposals. Those worried by the publicity surrounding the Lanica Trust approach had been told that the bank was not up for sale, he added.

Last month Co-operative News, the co-operative movement's newspaper, said carpet-baggers -- a term applied to many who have opened building society accounts to gain from their demutualisation -- were applying for membership in droves.
Shares in Lanica, which were star performers last year on speculation over Regan's intentions, were suspended on February 10 at 19.50 pounds each.
